claims.claim: James Maliszewski reports that Gygax demurred when told his voice was a dialect of Jack Vance's.
claims.quote: I once told Gary my opinion on this and he demurred

claims.claim: James Maliszewski contrasts Gygax's florid prose with modern game books, which he says read like technical manuals.
claims.quote: Modern game books read like what they are: technical manuals.

claims.claim: James Maliszewski holds up Gygax's description of the Vault of the Drow as more evocative than the place descriptions in contemporary adventures.
claims.quote: you'll find few passages in contemporary adventures that are as evocative

claims.claim: Dyson Logos tells OSR adventure writers to get rid of boxed text.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: So, OSR adventure writers, get rid of the boxed text.

claims.claim: Dyson Logos proposes replacing read-aloud prose with a point-form list of the things seen in the room, so the DM can present them conversationally.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: replace it with a point-form list of things seen in the room

claims.claim: Dyson Logos traces the arrival of read-aloud text in the 1e era to the tournament use of the early published adventures.
claims.source: Dyson Logos, 'The Dreaded Boxed Text', Dyson's Dodecahedron, 2013
claims.quote: I tend to blame this on the tournament usage

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says the number one complaint about published adventures is that they are hard to run.
claims.quote: The number one complaint about published adventures

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch distinguishes writing for oneself, where the words are only a memory cue, from writing for a stranger.
claims.quote: The words on the page are only a memory cue

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch attributes dry and tedious encounters to the failed transfer of the writer's imagined scene into the reader's head.
claims.quote: leading to dry and tedious encounters

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch frames his book as advice on writing an adventure for publication rather than for one's own table.
claims.quote: This book is advice on how to write an adventure for publication.

claims.claim: Courtney Campbell's key format admits no word that is not important.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash, 2012
claims.quote: Any word that is not important, is not used.

claims.claim: Courtney Campbell's key replaces prose with bolded nouns, and he says he describes a room using only the bolded words.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash, 2012
claims.quote: When describing things, I only use the bolded words!

claims.claim: Courtney Campbell reports that his key gives him everything needed to run the tick encounter in seven words.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash, 2012
claims.quote: everything I need to run the encounter successfully in seven words

claims.claim: In Courtney Campbell's format the items placed after the bar are the ones immediately visible on entering.
claims.source: Courtney Campbell, 'On Set Design', Hack & Slash, 2012
claims.quote: After the bar are the immediately visible items!

claims.claim: Gabor Lux credits the classic modules with terse simplicity and language that is expressive but functional.
claims.source: Gabor Lux (Melan), 'OSR Module O1: Against the Ultra-Minimalism', Beyond Fomalhaut, 2017
claims.quote: terse simplicity, expressive but functional language, play-oriented presentation
